speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is quite an act to follow but I will try.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, an industrial policy in finance may seem a contradiction in terms, but it is not.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The most consequential 20th century financial industrial policy was built by the British on the then undisputed reserve asset – the United States (US) dollar.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once, in 1933, the US imposed Regulation Q, capping interest rates that American banks could pay.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By the late 1960s, the ceiling was 4%, while three-month Treasury Bills approached 7%.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dollars held offshore, especially in London, escaped this cap.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This offshore dollar market became known as the Euro dollar market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When G-10 central banks proposed international regulation in the 1970s, the Bank of England blocked it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Central banks provided official deposits of 20% of net market and currency swaps with domestic banks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, after the 1974 banking crises, the G-10 Basel communiqué constructed an implicit lender-of-last-resort guarantee.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The result: London became the global centre for dollar financing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By the mid-1980s, there were more Euro dollars than dollars.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Euro dollar market increased the appeal of dollar holdings, deepening the liquidity for American borrowing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This privileged position, London held for many decades.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What is instructive is that the British reinvented London's proposition amidst the decline of sterling.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Then, interest rate caps created a push factor for the world's reserve asset to move offshore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is custody risk – the question of whether your reserves are still yours when the politics turn; and the emerging reserve asset seeking an offshore home is not dollars.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, access to funds has become conditional on political alignment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We rightly condemn the invasion of Ukraine, but the knock-on effect on Western financial centrality is real.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, market participants are pricing in US asset risk in a way they did not before the 2020s.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What makes this structural is the price insensitivity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There are few good alternatives for a reserve asset.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Central banks bought at $2,000 an ounce, at $3,000 an ounce, at $4,000 an ounce.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But if gold is becoming a reserve asset, it will need to be financialised.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Later, I will describe what that means in five pillars.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, let us assess some major gold hubs of today.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: London is the central gold pricing venue and is one of the world's major custodians for the world's central banks, via the Bank of England vaults.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It offers unmatched liquidity for gold, especially for the 400 oz "large bars" used by central banks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is the home of the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), which controls the global "good delivery" standard.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This certificate is important for liquidity amongst major financial centres.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In February 2022, after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the G7 immobilised $300 billion in Russian central bank reserves within weeks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The LBMA suspended all six Russian refiners from the Good Delivery list.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The message: custody and market access are conditional on political alignment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Germany, Hungary, Turkey and the Netherlands have done the same over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The case of New York is a puzzle.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In the lead-up to Liberation Day in April 2025, as tariff fears spiked, the exchange-for-physical (EFP) basis, which is the spread between New York COMEX futures and London over-the-counter (OTC) gold, blew out to $60 per ounce – the widest since the 2020 COVID-19 panic.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This led to COMEX vaults in New York hitting a record 43 million ounces.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For a moment, most of the world's financialised gold was in New York, rather than its typical home in London.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: New York had custody over both today's reserve asset and tomorrow's, simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A US Federal Reserve (the Fed) gold repo window, accepting COMEX gold warrants as collateral.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Strong financing terms could have made New York the permanent home for monetary gold, since much of it was already in COMEX vaults.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Now, it is true that the Fed conventionally runs repo backstops on Treasuries, agency debt and agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But that is already an expanded listing over pure Treasuries, pre-2008.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They had the moment – and did not act.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, there is no appetite, not yet, to backstop gold in New York.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Deep markets, but no lender of last resort.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Asset holders must also weigh the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) tail risk.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The executive powers used to impose tariffs in February 2025 could be turned on foreign-held assets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, only the US can offer a sovereign repo on gold as they have the reserve currency.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, if they do not backstop gold, financialisation will likely not proceed on single sovereign rails.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dubai is closest to what we could build.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Aggressive infrastructure: vaults, multiple refineries, direct African sourcing and the natural catchment of India.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is estimated that Dubai handles upwards of 15% of global physical gold trade.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dubai offers proximity to supply and demand, but also to Gulf conflict dynamics.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore offers a trusted node to multiple parties.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dubai has captured volume partly through more permissive sourcing standards.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is not our game – our competitive advantage is rigor and any visible compliance failure on money-laundering would destroy the credibility we hope to sell.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The shift to gold is large enough for multiple hubs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Gan said in response to my January Parliamentary Question about critical minerals financing, that the Government will act "when there is sufficient market interest." Well, the interest is here.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Mint launched its Lion Bullion line in September, explicitly citing strong investor demand.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Private vaults are expanding: The Reserve opened last year with capacity for 15,500 tonnes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In that same Parliamentary Question I posed to the Ministry of Trade and Industry in January, I asked why our framework for metal warrant financing is under-utilised.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The response from the Ministry framed it in terms of the base metals, by referring to the London Metal Exchange (LME) ecosystem, which handles the six primary base metals – copper, zinc, aluminum, nickel, lead, tin.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I had in mind gold, not base metals.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Gold operates through the LBMA – different rules, different warehousing, different settlement – and requires purpose-built architecture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have one LBMA-approved refinery – Metalor, Swiss-owned.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Central Provident Fund members investing in gold through SPDR Gold Shares will see that gold held in London and New York vaults.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What is puzzling is that Singapore also seems to be on the other side of the trend.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Keep in mind that this was when gold, averagely, was about US$3,300 per troy oz.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Gold today trades at US$5,000 per troy oz, 50% higher than where MAS was sold it, if this report is true.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, could the Government confirm whether this is true?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If so, why does it hold such a contrarian view relative to most global central banks?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Does it have a framework for thinking about gold's role in tomorrow's reserve system?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The core asset Singapore can offer is not location or tax rates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is legal predictability – the credible commitment that asset treatment follows established judicial process, not executive discretion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In January 2020, Singapore enacted the International Organisations (Immunities and Privileges) (Bank for International Settlements) Order.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It states that property and assets entrusted to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), quote, "wherever located, by whomsoever held and in whatever format, are immune from search, requisition, confiscation, expropriation or any other form of seizure, taking or foreclosure, by any form of legal process." That is the gold standard, forgive the expression, for custody protection.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore should consider a Reserves Custody Protection Act, or an amendment to the MAS Act, establishing that custody arrangements are governed by Singapore law and due process, immunising it from executive discretion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should be a top choice for jurisdictions seeking diversified custody.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Sovereign guarantees are best implemented via sovereign vaults in the same vein as the Bank of England, rather than outsourcing capacity to private parties, as Zurich has done.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MAS reserves held in Singapore vaults create the base load that foreign participants need to see.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Euro dollar market had central banks providing 20% of net demand.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is one thing to have custody, but to have trusted custody requires the above.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To connect these markets, you need recasting capacity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dubai built multiple refineries with no mining industry.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should expand refining capacity and establish direct relationships with miners in Africa, Australia, Indonesia, and strengthen existing ones with the bullion banks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Precious metals streaming – providing upfront capital to miners in exchange for future production at agreed prices – is one proven vehicle for building those relationships.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Tungsten has nearly identical density to gold – counterfeits exist.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2020, China's Kingold was accused of pledging gilded-copper "gold" as collateral for 20bn yuan in loans, turning "gold receipts" into a major credit-fraud event.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Robust verification through X-ray Fluorescence (XRF) and ultrasound should be part of the chain, if possible, non-destructively to preserve provenance, but if necessary, destructively by recasting.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not just "is it stored?" but "is it real?" Singapore should build a reputation for rigorous verification that makes our warehouse receipts bankable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And in our warehouses or vaults, we need strong verification standards, to be able to financialise a wide net of gold collateral, the LBMA-approved and those outside the LBMA system alike.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Digital warehouse receipts issued under Singapore standards should be legally enforceable claims.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The LBMA sets the global Good Delivery standard.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should aim to make our standard inter-operable with LBMA, possibly as a custody wrapper on top of LBMA.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate: within the CME Group, gold receives different treatment depending on standard.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: COMEX warrants are valid collateral for customer accounts, while London LBMA bullion is not.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We would be selling liquidity: the guarantee that gold with the Singapore custody stamp can be used as collateral, that banks will lend against it, that it trades on major exchanges.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Beyond custody: liquid markets for price discovery and financing against verified collateral.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We can be a multicurrency hub for gold financing – swapping it for US dollar, renminbi, or other currencies of choice.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: GOFO was the benchmark interest rate at which banks lent gold.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Its main practical use was enabling interest rate swaps on gold.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Consider a gold producer hedging future production over five years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The conventional instrument is a long-dated forward – locking in a price to sell gold years from now.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The problem is that if gold moves from $3,000 to $5,000, the mark-to-market between counterparties swings accordingly, and that exposure sits unsettled for years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The result is large, volatile collateral calls and significant counterparty credit risk.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: An interest rate swap solves this by separating the hedge into two components.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The price exposure is hedged with short-dated instruments that settle frequently, so credit exposure resets regularly and never accumulates over years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The cost-of-carry component is hedged via the swap, which is long-dated but insensitive to the spot price, keeping its mark-to-market small and stable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The combined position achieves the same economic result as the forward, but with a fraction of the counterparty exposure.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That means smaller collateral calls, lower capital requirements for banks – and a more efficient market overall.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This would give banks the pricing infrastructure to build gold financing capabilities here.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Even if gold's share of reserves stabilises rather than continues to climb, the infrastructure I describe is not wasted.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Gold is the use case with the most immediate demand, but the platform outlasts any single price cycle.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The British built the Euro dollar market through deliberate policy – forbearance, defence, direct participation, implicit guarantees – at a moment when sterling was in decline and the world's reserve asset was looking for an offshore home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our financial centre was built too on deliberate pillars: rule of law, institutional trust, regulatory predictability.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Hedge funds we incubated are opening in Dubai.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dubai's financial centre doubled its hedge fund count to over a hundred in a single year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They will move on the next thing before we have formed a committee to study it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is not the nature of the standards, but the structural bet.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore won a windfall when Hong Kong shut itself down during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Jobs, institutional knowledge, relevance – those are the stakes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Rule of law, institutions, trust – these are necessary conditions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Other cities have learned to offer versions of the same, combined with speed we have not matched.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it is the question: can Singapore still see a structural shift in the global financial system and build for it, or have we become the kind of country that convenes a review after the opportunity has passed?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Because once you become mediocre, derivative, content to be a fast-adopter, there is no bottom to that market.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is no disagreement with what he has laid out in terms of our ambition.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Indeed, that is also something that my colleagues and I in MAS have been looking at, to see what are the opportunities that we can capture, not just in the gold market, but across different parts of the financial centre, which as he mentioned, is multi-faceted, multi-dimensional.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It had started some decades ago and what we have achieved today is the result of sound policy choices, discipline, governance and a long-term view of how finance can serve our economy, our companies and our people.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is because of many years of hard work, together with the industry, that we have put in place these pillars of strength.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Several factors have underpinned this positive outcome, which has benefited Singapore and many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, Asia's continued growth and sustained development over the years have created strong demand for capital and international companies which are keen to tap into the region's growth opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has led to financing opportunities for financial institutions and investment opportunities for both global investors who are seeking access to Asian markets and also Asian investors who are looking to diversify their portfolios globally.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, a sound and progressive regulatory regime, which safeguards financial stability and ensures that financial institutions in Singapore adhere to high prudential and regulatory standards and practices.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think we recognise the different financial centres will have different market niches that they want to target, different strengths that they play to.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And Singapore's strengths and Dubai's strengths may not be exactly the same, the markets that we target may not be exactly the same.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I think the international financial markets, the scale is large enough for there to be more than one international financial sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, Dubai can be a strong, good financial centre and so can we.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we can serve different roles, serve different customers and we both grow together.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS has been working closely with the industry on this so that we know what the opportunities are and therefore, what are some of the policies that we will have to look at.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, we granted banking licences to four digital banks, which have added diversity and competition to our banking system and provided consumers and also underserved segments of population with greater product offerings.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A second example is our FinTech Regulatory Sandbox, which enables firms to experiment with innovative products and business models in a controlled regulatory environment, within time-bound relaxations and subject to appropriate safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This encourages experimentation while containing risk, helping firms to innovate by taking calculated risks and also pushing the boundaries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our competitive edge lies in developing a strong core of local talent as well as attracting complementary professionals from abroad.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This combination allows us to build an internationally competitive and innovative financial ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have been driving the development of Singapore's financial sector for many years.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, deepening our strengths in key asset classes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are working with the industry to expand these capabilities, including in private equity and private credit, to better serve the growth capital needs across Asia.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, strengthening horizontal enablers, such as the use of technology.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through various grants, MAS has supported the establishment of over 15 innovation labs by our financial institutions and major technology players.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this has funded more than 50 projects and proof-of-concepts, including in artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technology and cross-border payment linkages with regional partners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These initiatives enable financial institutions to harness technology to stay competitive in a rapidly changing industry.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: People are at the heart of everything we do, and the financial sector is a key provider of good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS has launched schemes to build workforce competencies, and to develop specialist talents and leaders in finance.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, in partnership with the industry, we have trained over 8,000 finance professionals in sustainable finance, covering priority roles, such as credit risk analysts and corporate banking relationship managers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are also uplifting and upskilling our workforce to make good use of AI, helping our institutions to harness technology to augment jobs and enabling our workers to be more productive so that they can do higher value-added work.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We adopt a collaborative approach which ensures that policies and development initiatives are aligned with market realities and can play to our strengths.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And one of Singapore's strengths, which investors look to, is that we are a trusted place, stable and they can make long-term plans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, I think, in what we do, we have got to bear that in mind.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because that is what differentiates us from other financial centres.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore's financial sector has made much progress over the years as a trusted global hub and international financial centre.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we are certainly not resting on our laurels, and we are not done building and growing our financial services industry.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We believe that there is still a lot more we can do and the way that we want to move forward is to work very closely with our industry, because I believe that is also one of our strengths.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The barriers between the Government and the industry here in Singapore, we do not have very tall and rigid barriers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We work very closely with our industry partners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of the things that we try may not succeed, but we must try.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And for those that we try and succeed, it may allow us to take off.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And in the end, benefit our economy, benefit our companies but most importantly, benefit our people.
